analysis.one_liner: Makes Endangered Species Act penalties require intent, advance notice, and a correction period, and shields compliant landowners.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had no cosponsors, was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and never received a vote before the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten how the Endangered Species Act is enforced. It would have required that a person knowingly and intentionally harm a protected species before facing any civil or criminal penalty, given violators official notice and 30 days to stop or fix the harm before penalties could apply, and let defendants escape enforcement by arguing they couldn't reasonably have known the animal or plant involved was protected. It would also have barred the government from demanding extra mitigation from landowners who follow an approved conservation plan, and created 'safe harbor' agreements giving landowners grants of up to $10,000 to restore habitat.
analysis.who_benefits: Landowners, developers, and businesses whose activities incidentally harm protected species would gain the most. They could only be penalized if they acted knowingly and intentionally, would get a warning and a 30-day window to fix violations before owing anything, and could defend themselves in court or in citizen suits by saying they didn't know the species was protected. Landowners who sign conservation plans would be locked into no additional mitigation costs without their consent, and individual private landowners could receive grants of up to $10,000 for safe harbor agreements.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Landowners, developers, and businesses facing ESA penalties

how_it_helps.text: The bill would redefine a prohibited 'take' of a protected species to require that a person knowingly and intentionally performed an act they knew would harass, harm, or kill a listed species, or attempted to do so — a much higher bar than current law, which does not require intent.

A person conducting an otherwise lawful activity not aimed at taking a species would owe no criminal or civil penalty unless the Secretary of the Interior gave them notice of the violation and they failed to correct it within 30 days.

It would create an affirmative defense in enforcement actions and citizen suits for defendants who could not reasonably have known the fish, wildlife, or plant involved was a member of an endangered or threatened species.

Landowners in compliance with an approved conservation plan could not be required, without their consent, to undertake additional mitigation measures or land-use restrictions beyond what the plan already requires.

The bill would authorize 'safe harbor' agreements under which landowners agree to create, restore, or improve habitat in exchange for permission to incidentally take species back to an agreed baseline, with grants of up to $10,000 per individual private landowner.

analysis.who_pays: The cost falls on protected wildlife and the public that relies on the Endangered Species Act's protections: accidental or negligent harm to listed species would largely become unenforceable, violators could keep harming a species for at least 30 days after being noticed, and mitigation commitments would be frozen at whatever a conservation plan originally promised. Taxpayers would fund the landowner grants, though the bill caps them at $10,000 per landowner and makes them subject to appropriations.

drawbacks.text: Requiring knowing and intentional conduct, notice, and a 30-day correction period means accidental, negligent, or indirect killing of protected species would generally carry no penalty, which conservation groups warned makes incidental harm to endangered species essentially unenforceable.

The 'no surprises' provision would lock in the terms of a conservation plan permanently, preventing the government from requiring new mitigation even if a species' condition worsens, except under 'extraordinary circumstances' the plan itself must define.

The affirmative defense for defendants who could not reasonably have known a species was listed would weaken not just government enforcement but also the citizen suits that private citizens use to enforce the Act.

Supporters would acknowledge that the bill also included genuine conservation tools — safe harbor agreements and habitat-restoration grants — so its costs to enforcement were the price of those incentives.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's safe harbor agreements and landowner grants are real, tested conservation incentives that reward landowners for restoring habitat. But those are the smaller part of the bill. Its main changes — an intent requirement, notice plus a 30-day cure period, an ignorance defense, and a freeze on new mitigation obligations — would have made the Endangered Species Act dramatically harder to enforce against landowners and businesses whose activities incidentally kill protected species. On balance, the enforcement changes would outweigh the conservation incentives for anyone who cares about protecting listed wildlife.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced, got no cosponsors and no committee action, and died there when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Rep. William Thomas introduced the bill on September 11, 1998, near the end of the 105th Congress, and delivered introductory remarks the same day.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Resources on the day of introduction and never advanced to a markup, a floor vote, or any other action.
No other member cosponsored the bill.
The 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, and the bill died in committee without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Existing Endangered Species Act enforcement stayed fully intact, so conservationists and the public kept the status quo; landowners and developers did not get the liability shield they would have gained had it passed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public kept existing species protections

for.name: Rep. William M. Thomas
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on September 11, 1998, gave introductory remarks, and referred it to the Resources Committee.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote and drew no cosponsors, so there is no record of how either party would have lined up for or against it.

industries.industry: Real estate developers and commercial landowners
industries.note: The bill would have shielded them from civil and criminal penalties for incidental harm to protected species unless they acted knowingly and intentionally, and would have frozen conservation-plan obligations so no new mitigation costs could be added. Their gain comes directly at the expense of species protections the public relies on.

industries.industry: Agriculture, timber, and other land-intensive industries
industries.note: The intent requirement, notice-and-cure period, and ignorance defense would have made it far harder to enforce the Endangered Species Act against routine farming, ranching, and logging operations that incidentally harm listed species. 'No surprises' language would also prevent new land-use restrictions from being imposed mid-plan.

Individual landowners could receive grants of up to $10,000 to carry out safe harbor agreements that restore habitat, and the grants stack on top of existing farm conservation program payments. This is one part of the bill that benefits both landowners and wildlife.
The affirmative defense based on not knowing a species was listed would weaken both government enforcement actions and the citizen lawsuits ordinary people use to enforce species protections.
